message.content: I want to understand why the sky is blue at noon but red near sunset. My teacher said it has to do with light and air, but the explanation went by too fast.

Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color is a wave, and the colors differ in the length of their waves: blue waves are short and red waves are long. When light travels through the air, it meets gas molecules that are much smaller than a wavelength. These molecules push the light in all directions, and they push short waves far more strongly than long waves. Physicists call this scattering.

At noon the sun is high, and its light crosses only a thin layer of air to reach you. Blue light is scattered all over the sky, so when you look at any part of the sky away from the sun, some blue light arrives from that direction into your eyes. That is why the whole dome looks blue. Violet is scattered even more, but the sun gives less of it, and our eyes respond weakly to it, so we see blue.

At sunset the sun is low, and its light must cross a much longer path through the air. Along that path, most of the blue light has already been scattered out of the beam and sent in other directions. What remains is mostly orange and red, and these colors reach your eyes straight from the sun and from the clouds that it lights from below. Dust and smoke can make the effect stronger, which is why sunsets after a dry summer or a large fire can look especially deep red.
Does the same idea explain why the moon sometimes looks orange when it is low?

Yes, it is the same effect. Moonlight is only sunlight reflected from a gray surface, so it has the same mixture of colors. When the moon sits near the horizon, its light crosses a long path through the lower, thicker and dustier air, and the blue part is scattered away before it reaches you. What is left looks yellow or orange. As the moon climbs, the path becomes shorter and the color returns to a pale white. Try to look at it on a clear evening and again two hours later.
